This research paper presents a novel integrated data and energy transmission network that incorporates D2D communication, with a focus on the presence of an IRS-assisted D2D link. The IRS is modeled as having adjustable phase and reflective phase shift adjustments for all its elements, with a specific formula used to determine the optimal configuration for maximizing the IRS's overall efficiency. The results show that this model significantly improves system performance when compared to non-IRS assisted systems.

The surge in demand for online training in experimental fluid dynamics has led to the development of a remote-controlled LDV system. This new setup enables researchers to conduct experiments in the laboratory without being physically present, by utilizing a remote connection to operate the equipment and collect data. This document outlines the design and implementation of a remotely controlled LDV system using a specific software package and commercially available hardware components. The document also presents two-dimensional velocity field measurements obtained from a channel flow experiment, demonstrating the feasibility and accuracy of operating LDV data acquisition remotely.

The cardinality of models for sentences in first-order logic with a particular set of relations can be determined precisely using first-order expressible properties, but with models containing more than three types of relations, this is not the case, even with the restriction to sentences containing only three variables, even with models containing only three types of relations, this is not the case either.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is being explored in 
improving the image quality of transmission electron microscopes. By manipulating 
the electron wave's amplitude and phase, these phase plates can enhance contrast 
and resolve finer details. Our research focuses on utilizing a custom-designed 
programmable phase plate to correct for the natural blurring that occurs in TEMs, 
caused by the instrument's point spread function. A high-resolution target 
image is first captured in the TEM, then an optimized phase plate correction is 
applied to recover the original sample's features. Computer simulations and 
experimental trials demonstrate the potential for our phase plate to significantly 
improve image clarity and detail recovery.

Building on von Neumann's work, we introduce the concept of quantum measurement and computation within the framework of category theory. This involves developing a new category, known as the measurement category, derived from a specific type of category called dagger compact category. The measurement category enables the formulation of a universal theory of quantum computation, which, when applied to categorical quantum circuits, aligns with the existing established theory. Furthermore, the application of the measurement category to C*-categories yields a concept referred to as the measurement algebra, which encompasses the principles of quantum measurement and broadcasting, including the fundamental no-broadcasting theorem.

This paper provides an explicit formula for calculating the number of possible positions in a d-dimensional space, represented by the set $\mathbb{Z}^d$, after n steps of a random walk starting from the origin. The formula is derived using combinatorics and relies on the use of inclusion-exclusion principle. It ultimately involves summing products of binomial coefficients, which can be efficiently computed even for large values of n using dynamic programming. The position distribution resulting from this enumeration approach aligns with that of a well-known statistical distribution based on the Chernoff method.

This research delves into the extended geometry and quasinormal modes of a spherically symmetric polymer black hole with O'Raifeartaigh-Pullin-Gambini discrete spacetime structure, featuring a non-singular, constant, and positive minimal length parameter. By applying the WKB approximation, we compute the quasinormal frequencies for this polymer black hole and find that, in the limit of large frequencies, the quasinormal spectrum aligns with that of a standard Schwarzschild black hole. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of the minimal length parameter on the quasinormal frequencies and find a linear relationship between the real part of the frequencies and the square of this parameter for fixed imaginary frequencies.

We have developed a theoretical model to calculate thermal properties of doped graphene sheets, taking into account thermal effects. Analyzing frequency and momentum dependence, we found that thermal screening reduces interparticle interactions in doped graphene, allowing us to calculate heat capacity and find that its behavior at high temperatures is linearly related to the cube of the temperature.

Our proposed MaskedSpeech model utilizes a novel masking strategy in a Transformer-based architecture for context-aware speech synthesis. This model employs a method where adjacent audio segments are sequentially masked and predicted, alternating with panning operations. The masking strategy significantly enhances synthesis performance with minimal computational overhead. Additionally, our research explores the impact of masking size on synthesis quality and presents a novel approach to cross-entropy loss for improved performance. The model's exceptional synthesis quality and robustness are demonstrated through comprehensive evaluations.

We've developed a projection predictive approach that initially utilizes a high-dimensional model to capture key uncertainties, then progressively eliminates non-essential variables to transfer this knowledge into a simplified inference model. This inference model, updated using Bayesian methods, provides reliable uncertainty estimates for new data points. We've applied it to various regression problems, both with and without predefined transformations of the data, and demonstrated its effectiveness by comparing it to related projection predictive techniques and high-dimensional modeling strategies through extensive simulations.

Recent breakthroughs in the capabilities of generative models have led to their integration into a range of applications, including classification tasks. However, the potential for abuse by malicious actors remains a significant concern, as they could leverage flawed classifiers to manipulate systems. This study investigates the vulnerability of classifiers to in-between attacks launched by malicious generative models, examining their ability to generate clean labels for testing data. We develop a theoretical framework for modeling these attacks and compare multiple malicious generative models, including variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks. Our analysis reveals that intermediate attacks can be both more effective and computationally more efficient than traditional model poisoning methods.

Climate change conspiracy theories are being spread online, but research on the topic is limited. This study focuses on conspiracy theories related to climate change by examining their presence on social media. We analyzed nearly 10,000 tweets containing the term "climate change conspiracy" to understand their characteristics. Our findings reveal a diverse group of people engaging with these conspiracy theories, with a significant portion originating from the far-left political spectrum. We identified 11 distinct narratives being shared, with some promoting the idea that climate change is fabricated to protect the oil industry, while others suggest that it's a government conspiracy to control people's lives. Our research also highlights the challenges in detecting these conspiracy theories using automated methods, as they often use the same language as mainstream views on climate change.

A study of dark matter production in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV is conducted using data from the CMS experiment at CERN. The analysis focuses on events containing a top quark, either in pairs or alongside a single top quark, and significant amounts of invisible energy. The data collected correspond to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb^-1. The results are compared to predictions without dark matter, and no evidence for its presence is found. The findings are translated into limits on the strength of interactions between dark matter and Standard Model particles in models that involve dimension-6 operators, and also on the mass and coupling of a mediator particle in a model that involves a top quark-flipped variant of a supersymmetric model that does not have R-parity.

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based angles. We also determine a specific condition necessary for the presence of Serre duality. Assuming duality exists, we establish a one-to-one correspondence involving a bijection and specific category characteristics.

The study examines the impact of fields of study on earnings using an estimated joint distribution of earnings and occupation-specific skills. An analytical framework is developed to address challenges in measuring treatment effects when the chosen field of study has an ordinal nature. It is demonstrated that return rates vary based on field-specific and occupation-specific factors. A potential solution is presented, which relies on field-instrumented individuals and assumes that fields with similar characteristics produce graduates with comparable skills. The validity of this assumption is tested empirically. The study finds significant returns to fields of study, which are substantial when considering the overall population. However, these gains are concentrated among those whose fields of study align with their occupations.

The potential of high-energy particle collisions to produce rare antiparticles,
specifically antineutrons, has long been of great interest due to their unique
properties. A new approach to producing these particles using super $J/\psi$
collisions offers a revolutionary method to create large quantities of
antineutrons, which can then be used for advanced nuclear and particle physics
research. This technique, involving the precise measurement of the produced
particles, allows for the generation of antineutrons with extremely low energies,
which can be used for cutting-edge experiments. This includes not only the
production of antineutrons, but also a range of other exotic particles such as
antiprotons, $\Sigma^+$ baryons, and $\Xi^-$ baryons, which can be used for
advanced nuclear and particle physics research. The potential of this approach
is further illustrated by examples of its application to the creation of
antimatter-based optical lattices and the production of antihydrogen atoms.
The precision of the produced antineutrons, along with the ability to precisely
control their production, offers the possibility of making significant
advancements in our understanding of these elusive particles.

Theoretical models of hierarchical triple systems with binary accretors and surrounding discs have not been thoroughly investigated. We conducted numerical simulations using the smoothed particle hydrodynamics method to model the interaction between a surrounding gas cloud and a binary-orbiting system consisting of two smaller binaries. The simulations revealed that accretion rates onto the binary system exhibit irregular fluctuations, which are influenced by the relative orientation and orbital dynamics between the binary system and the surrounding gas cloud. We identified key factors that affect accretion rates, including the angle between the binary orbits and the surrounding gas cloud, as well as the ratio of angular momentum between the binary orbit and the surrounding gas cloud. The simulations also revealed that accretion rates can be significantly higher or lower than expected based on standard Eddington-Switching models, which could have implications for the formation and evolution of planetary systems.

This study examines flat spacetime models that approximate the behavior of a flat universe by considering a lattice structure made up of identical, space-filling cells. Each cell in the model consists of a dual tetrahedron and a cube, linked together at their centers. An analysis demonstrates that the models are intrinsically flat, possessing a zero intrinsic curvature, yet they exhibit non-zero extrinsic curvature at the lattice nodes. By calculating these curvatures, the model's energy-momentum tensor is derived, indicating characteristics aligned with those of dark energy.

This study presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model that integrates the technical advancements in image restoration. The initial phase of the model denoises the input image using a restoration approach, taking into account the specific characteristics of the noise. A level-set based active contour model is then employed in the second stage to segment the denoised image, while efficiently handling moving boundaries. The proposed method was successfully tested on synthetic and real-world images, demonstrating its capability to achieve high-quality image segmentation results.

The mechanism of superradiance has the potential to create a cloud of ultralight particles, which can interact with celestial bodies and cause observable effects, particularly in the spin alignments of heavy quasars. Our research focuses on a heavy quasar, specifically U1508A, which exhibits a spin alignment consistent with the superradiance hypothesis. By analyzing observational data, we establish a range of masses for the particles involved, which falls between 10^-20 and 10^-17 eV, a range that contradicts previous estimates derived from other experiments.

Our approach utilizes an open-source neural network simulator to develop a virtual representation of the neuromorphic chip Loihi, allowing us to analyze its underlying mechanisms and evaluate its performance potential. By doing so, we can gain insight into the advantages of analog computation in mixed-signal circuits and make more informed design decisions.

A notable solar type II noise storm was documented in 2013, originating from a small active region on the far side of the sun. The source of this storm exhibited correlated shifts in both frequency and duration as a result of the gradual loss of magnetic field strength. This observation aligns with the theory that the storm frequency is directly linked to the magnetic field strength. The data also suggest that the storm duration is influenced by the time it takes for the Alfvén wave to travel, which in turn is affected by the magnetic field strength. The study also reveals that the magnetic field configuration played a crucial role in the emission process, with field lines that were twisted and sheared producing the most intense and frequent radio bursts. The researchers also noted that the magnetic field strength affected the emission characteristics of the burst, with stronger fields resulting in longer and more frequent bursts.

A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, one that is integrated into a two-dimensional plane, by utilizing a previously created kit of layered materials. This trap design features specific components, including a beam-splitting material, half-silvered, to direct both optical pumping and magnetic fields within a confined area. A particular kit, composed of printed material layers, is used both as a structural support and a functional part of the trap's integration. A test Rb atom cloud experiment demonstrated the effectiveness of this in-plane MOET, exhibiting good spatial confinement and comparable polarisation to traditional trap systems.

The spherically symmetric collapse of a relativistic, pressureless accretion cloud onto a supermassive black hole is analyzed for various initial radii and specific angular momentum distributions. It's discovered that for a finite-sized cloud, density build-up near the horizon only occurs when the initial radius is at least around 1000 times the gravitational radius. This increase in required size is attributed to angular momentum conservation, which prevents infalling matter from reaching the black hole. As a result, our findings suggest that spherically symmetric models may not be suitable for describing long-term black hole mass growth in certain environments, such as the growth of supermassive black holes.

The excitation probabilities and emitted radiation from an otherwise ground-state atom, influenced by both thermal and vacuum electromagnetic fields, are investigated in the context of the atom moving in space following a sudden acceleration. The atom's subsequent radiation patterns are analyzed in the time domain following recoil, with additional calculations in the frequency domain revealing that its emitted radiation consists of two distinct components: one induced by the atom's acceleration and another resulting from its uniform motion.

A comprehensive study of the massive star population surrounding Westerlund 2 has been conducted, focusing on the HII regions WDC02484-6452 and WDC02484-6453. These areas contain numerous O and OF stars, with a total of 13 and 17, respectively. Spectral analysis of these stars revealed significant variability in their spectral types, with some stars classified as early O-type and others exhibiting characteristics of late O or Of types. The spatial distribution of these stars is distinct, with Westerlund 2 located at the center of WDC02484-6452, and the remaining stars located in WDC02484-6453. The analysis of Gaia parallax data revealed that Westerlund 2 lies at a distance of approximately 20-25 kpc, with a notable exception of star HD 153328, which lies at a significantly greater distance. The analysis of proper motion data revealed that Westerlund 2 lies at a significantly greater distance than previously thought, with a notable exception of star HD 153328. This paper investigates the normalized ground state solution for the given biharmonic Choquard equation: $-\Delta^2 u+\beta\Delta u =\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^4} |y|^{\sigma_2}\phi_{\alpha}( |x-y|^2 )|u|^p\right) |x|^{-\sigma_2}\phi_{\alpha}(u)^{*}_pu.$ We demonstrate the existence of such a solution under specific conditions for the parameters $\beta$, $\sigma_2$, and the exponent $p$.

Degraded handwritten documents, affected by poor ink quality, image distortion, low resolution, and color shift, can be challenging to read and interpret. These issues are particularly pronounced in historical documents. Current image enhancement techniques, however, are limited by their reliance on handwritten text lines and struggle with word and character-level transformations. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel approach centered on handwritten word images. This involves developing a multi-task adversarial network that can effectively transform real degraded word images into realistic enhanced ones. The network's design incorporates a character-level generative adversarial network to improve single character synthesis and a content-aware generative adversarial network to preserve fine-grained details. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing image enhancement techniques on both synthetic and real-world handwritten word images.

The growth of paper-based documentation has led to an accumulation of documents that are difficult to access, hindering data retrieval and search capabilities. To mitigate this issue, a proposed solution involves utilizing an ID card extractor that leverages computer vision and natural language technologies to gather and consolidate essential information from Indonesian identity cards. By integrating a hybrid of Convolutional Neural Networks and Conditional Random Fields, the extractor's performance has been demonstrated to achieve a 94% accuracy rate in a controlled setting. Furthermore, the efficacy of rule-based post-processing in enhancing overall performance is also substantiated.

In IEEE 802.11p standard, channel estimation is performed using a pilot-based method which leads to lower accuracy due to a lower number of pilots. Although various channel estimation techniques have been proposed to improve accuracy, they often come with higher complexity. This paper proposes a lower complexity temporal averaging channel estimation technique based on an LSTM model that can operate within the IEEE 802.11p standard framework. By utilizing the entire data packet for channel estimation, our proposed method surpasses traditional techniques in terms of performance.

We've developed a method using a GAN-based image colorization technique to improve the quality of low-resolution, black-and-white astronomical images. The method builds on previous image colorization methods that use a CNN to learn the relationship between RGB images and their low-resolution, color equivalents. However, these methods often fail when presented with images that deviate from the training data distribution. To address this issue, we trained a U-Net based CNN for generating realistic RGB images from low-resolution grayscale inputs, using a dataset of 1000 SNe Ia images from the CNNTRAINER project. The colorization method's performance was further enhanced by incorporating a style transfer network that adapts the colorization model to individual monochromatic images, allowing it to accurately colorize images that were not included in the training data.

Optimizing neural networks often involves an inefficient process of adjusting parameters through backpropagation, which can be time-consuming and computationally expensive. In this research, we introduce an innovative machine learning framework that bypasses the need for gradient calculations during training. By leveraging the principles of the Universal Approximation Theorem, our method trains each layer independently, resulting in significantly reduced computational costs. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments comparing it to conventional methods, including backpropagation, in four different test cases. The results show that our method achieves comparable performance at a fraction of the computational cost.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Panel recently concluded its second term and published a comprehensive report detailing its activities during both periods. The report outlines the panel's organizational framework, composition, and primary objectives for both its first and second stints. Following the completion of its second term, the panel recommended the extension of its activities through the establishment of an advisory capacity for ECFA management.

Confining and directing-curved line waves on curved surfaces holds significant potential for advanced optical applications. However, achieving this in practice is complicated by the line waves' susceptibility to dispersion and radiation losses. A solution to these challenges involves a specialized optical metasurface with integrated waveguides, capable of effectively steering and confining line waves while minimizing dispersion and radiation effects.

A rapidly evolving field of multi-agent collaborative learning is driving the development of intelligent systems capable of learning from multiple humans and robots working together. Our research focuses on creating an advanced architecture that enables efficient learning from and adaptation to large datasets of collaborative human-robot interactions. By leveraging the power of Graph Convolutional Networks, our framework can uncover the complex relationships between agents and their actions, building a fundamental model of their interactions. This model serves as a basis for predicting and interpreting the behaviors of our adaptive system. Through rigorous testing on a diverse dataset of 15,000 collaborative interaction samples, our results demonstrate the significant potential of this approach in creating intelligent systems for applications such as adaptive tutoring systems.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been developed for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of inconsistent original estimates with nonparametric regressors. To achieve correction, a reduced mean absolute deviation method was implemented using a reduced sample size. The bias reduction is confirmed for both reduced and non-reduced estimators, which were then compared in terms of efficiency and statistical inference. Specifically, a nonparametric confidence interval for the conditional median was established and its performance was verified through simulation studies and real data analysis.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a common link in their objectives, allowing them to benefit from each other in a mutually reinforcing manner. To achieve this synergy, we have developed an integrated framework that simultaneously tackles both tasks by utilizing shared representations and cross-task interactions. As a result, our framework exhibits superior performance on various datasets for relation extraction and establishes a new benchmark for accuracy in knowledge graph link prediction.

The impact of anisotropy and baryonic density on complex quark systems, such as quarkonium, is investigated in our research. We calculate the dissociation properties of quarkonium by considering the combined effects of momentum anisotropy and finite baryonic chemical potential on the quasi-particle Debye mass. Our analysis reveals that the quarkonium binding energy decreases as the degree of momentum anisotropy increases, particularly at higher temperatures and densities. Conversely, we observe that the dissociation temperature rises with increasing density. Furthermore, we examine how the dissociation behavior changes with dimensionality and find that it becomes less pronounced in higher dimensions.

Our study of Tb3RuO7's properties revealed that it exhibits complex magnetic behavior with two transitions occurring at temperatures of 17.5 K and 4.5 K. The researchers discovered through neutron diffraction that at 1.8 K, Tb3RuO7 displays a magnetic structure composed of spin-3/2 Ru ions aligned in dimers and arranged in layers perpendicular to the ab plane. The internal magnetic fields affecting Ru ions are significantly higher than external fields above 2 Tesla, leading to a disorder within triangles formed by Ru ions. Additionally, the researchers observed that at temperatures below 4.5 K, Tb3RuO7 exhibits a magnetic structure composed of spin components aligned in directions parallel and anti-parallel to the c axis.

Deep learning models have been successful in capturing complex patterns, but their ability to generalize to unseen data is often limited. This is particularly evident when dealing with time series data that often exhibits time-invariant characteristics. In this study, we introduce a novel neural network design, featuring a locally connected structure that can efficiently process time series inputs and produce consistent, generalizable representations. This architecture is enhanced by a modulation mechanism, enabling the network to learn time-invariant, data-driven representations. As a result, our proposed method successfully addresses the challenge of time-invariant time series classification, outperforming existing approaches and demonstrating exceptional transferability across different datasets. Furthermore, our model's locally connected design has the potential to be applied to other tasks, such as local feature extraction and periodic signal recognition.

The challenge of adapting to distributional changes across various environments is a fundamental issue in machine learning. Current solutions rely heavily on a combination of semi-supervised learning techniques and causal concepts, but they are limited to simple scenarios with minor environmental variations. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel semi-supervised approach called semi-generative modeling, which generates pseudo-labels for unlabeled data by predicting unobserved environments. By integrating causal information, our method can effectively leverage both observed and latent data for robust covariate-shift adaptation. We demonstrate the efficacy of semi-generative modeling in providing reliable labels for unsupervised data, thereby outperforming existing techniques in a comprehensive evaluation.

Despite significant advancements in deep learning, there is still a lack of consensus on how deep learning models function effectively. In this paper, we aim to bridge this knowledge gap by providing a comprehensive overview of deep learning models, focusing on their geometric interpretations. Our approach involves a detailed examination of the relationships between data, features, and labels, as well as the functional blocks and structural frameworks of various deep learning models. By adopting a geometric perspective, we can gain deeper insights into the behavior of deep learning models, including the effects of data augmentation, inductive biases, and regularization techniques. Ultimately, our work serves as a reference guide for researchers and practitioners, enabling them to make more informed decisions about the application of deep learning models in different contexts.

We establish new lower limits on the square of the first Zagier lattice minimum ratio and demonstrate its convergence to a value slightly higher than one. This convergence is related to the principal factors of its associated modular group. These intermediate values correspond to the first lattice minimum ratios of specific, non-principal factors.

A research project aims to understand how deep learning-based jet taggers can be explained, by examining their reliance on various physical characteristics and their ability to capture complex relationships, in comparison to traditional boosting-based taggers. By utilizing high-performance jet substructure variables, deep learning taggers can be made to rely heavily on relevant characteristics, and can be found to capture non-linear relationships between these characteristics at an intermediate stage, although the final stage tends to rely more on basic variables linearly. By contrast, traditional boosting-based taggers tend to rely more on complex variables but are less effective at capturing relationships between these variables at an intermediate stage.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We introduce a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms when r equals zero or one. Our analysis explores various properties of this variation, including formulas for calculating it, established inequalities, bounds, and relationships with other mathematical expressions, such as a new identity and inequalities involving r-associated Stirling numbers. Additionally, a new method of inversion is presented, along with an examination of the characteristics of a particular matrix based on these Stirling numbers.

We have derived formulas for layer groups with ordinary and double character, overlaying one axis with either an ordinary or a gray vector. These group formulas enable the computation of irreducible representations, representation dimensions, and various domain wall properties. Additionally, we've developed a method to compute irreducible representations for these groups when acting on single electrons or pairs of electron holes.

Momentum operators corresponding to Killing vector fields on compact manifolds without boundary are examined within the context of quantum mechanics. It's demonstrated that for such fields, the commutator of associated momentum operators corresponds to a geometric invariant known as the Ricci tensor. Consequently, it's proven that for spheres and real projective spaces, the set of momentum operators is linearly dependent. Additionally, it's shown that for tori, the set of momentum operators associated with these Killing vector fields can form a basis for first-order differential operators that preserve the Laplacian, which in turn enables the construction of a spectrum-generating group for the Laplacian.

A sign problem arises in various Monte Carlo simulations when imaginary or complex interactions occur, leading to exponentially increasing computational costs with system size. Similarly, temporal sign problems can emerge due to unsuitable parameterization in imaginary-time path integrals, necessitating complex integration. A novel approach utilizing complex-valued neural networks has been developed to mitigate such issues, particularly in quantum spin models like the Hubbard model. By employing this method, a complex-valued parameterization ensures that unsampled configurations carry negligible statistical weight, thus eliminating the sign problem and allowing for the use of standard sampling techniques.

In this research, the concept of a composite Higgs is expanded to include the flavor sector, where the observed Higgs boson emerges from a mixing of fundamental and composite states within an extended Technicolor framework. The model's requirements are detailed in terms of the compositeness scale, the mixing parameters, and the mass of heavy vector-like fermions. The study also examines the implications on the flavor structure and the predictions made for compositeness effects within electroweak precision tests.

The immersive experience of VR has been limited by the absence of a sensory input, specifically tactile feedback. Although advancements in VR technology have led to the creation of haptic feedback systems, current solutions primarily offer positive interactions. Negative interactions in VR, however, can be exploited to create harmful tactile feedback, rendering users helpless and vulnerable to abuse. This paper explores the ethical implications of generating negative haptic feedback in VR, examining potential uses and dangers, as well as the potential for abuse by malicious actors. It also proposes mitigation strategies and a framework for regulating the creation and distribution of VR content that incorporates harmful haptic feedback.

To assess the potential of lesser-known languages in AI applications, this research investigates how well the BigScience model can be adapted to languages it hasn't been exposed to during training. By utilizing a single-word representation method and existing word-hyphenation resources, our experiment demonstrates that adding just one resource can significantly improve results, achieving a SARI score of 0.519 with English as the reference language for Guaraney, a South American indigenous language. Although the model's performance is limited by its representation capability, this study suggests that increasing the diversity of training data could lead to more effective AI applications for low-resource languages.

The binary star formation process is a complex and long-debated topic in astronomy.
Assuming star clusters originate from the collapse of massive molecular clouds,
theoretical models suggest that the initial mass of a binary system should increase
as the total mass of the collapsing core increases.
Using a numerical simulation based on a two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic model,
we investigated how the initial mass of a binary system changes with total core mass.
Our results indicate that the initial mass of a binary system initially increases
with total core mass up to a peak, after which it decreases.
This behavior can be attributed to the shift from core fragmentation to bulk collapse
as total core mass increases,
resulting in the formation of a single star or a binary system with a lower mass ratio.
Our findings suggest that the initial mass of a binary system may decrease
in certain conditions, contrary to previous assumptions.
This has significant implications for binary star formation and the distribution of stellar masses.

This research introduces the M-ar-Kanized-Faddeeva algorithm, an advanced method for decomposing complex datasets into distinct components through statistical analysis. Unlike traditional methods that rely on Gaussian models, our scheme leverages pre-integrated fast Fourier transforms to efficiently identify higher-order statistical relationships between components. By incorporating Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling and leveraging the Faddeeva function, the method achieves a significant reduction in computational complexity, scaling linearly with the number of data points. To further optimize performance, we develop a simplified variant of the algorithm, which we apply to various real-world datasets, including digital recordings, images, and simulated data.

The equivalence between the extended Polynomial Calculus and the Fixed Point Calculus with least fixed points, as established in prior research by H\"{o}hle and Vollmer (2019), can be leveraged to derive a simplified proof of a known result. Specifically, a more straightforward demonstration will be provided showing that PCP[O(log^2 n)] cannot solve the Graph Isomorphism problem.

A subring of a free associative algebra is $\sigma$-elementary if it can be generated by one algebra and $| \sigma|$ many subring elements. It has been proven that all primitive primitive rings are $\sigma$-elementary. We have found an infinite set of non-isomorphic subring elements that are not primitive but are elementary.

Social media platforms like Facebook and Twitter allow users to make assertions that cannot be definitively disproven, such as declaring themselves the best or implying superiority over others. Unfortunately, there's little incentive for claimants to be truthful, raising concerns about the veracity of such statements. In the absence of a method to verify these statements, we've developed an approach to analyze and categorize them, identifying underlying patterns that can be tested empirically. Our study focuses on a dataset of one million posts from the Twitter platform, examining claims that cannot be definitively disproven, and comparing them to those that can be verified. Our analysis reveals distinct structures within these unfalsifiable claims, allowing us to differentiate between them based on their content and provide a method for validating these claims, such as identifying specific indicators of superlative statements.

Social media events captured with location and time data can provide valuable insights into various events happening around the world. Unfortunately, most existing approaches either overlook the dynamic nature of event timelines or assume a static location for each detected event. In contrast, our research focuses on identifying events based on their spatio-temporal characteristics using a combination of probabilistic models and machine learning techniques. Our method employs a Hidden Markov Model to segment timelines into distinct parts and an advanced algorithm called Viterbi to pinpoint the start and end of each event. To address the challenge of noisy location data, we apply a clustering approach that allows events to occur across multiple locations over time. Our method is then evaluated using a publicly available dataset of real-world events and compared against a baseline approach. Experimental results show that our method outperforms the baseline in terms of accuracy and event detection capabilities.

This research introduces a fast method for computing the cosmic microwave background's B-mode polarization and galaxy large-scale structure's joint bispectrum. We utilize CMB lensing to link B-mode signals with matter distribution information, which in turn can constrain inflationary models more effectively than studying the CMB alone. We develop a technique to calculate the cross-bispectrum between CMB B-modes and galaxy large-scale structure across two specific redshifts with greater efficiency. Our analysis focuses on the optimal configuration for leveraging the CMB's superior angular resolution to enhance redshift bin selection. We then perform a forecast analysis, incorporating the optimal setup and optimal analysis weights, which reveals that our method can achieve approximately 10 times better results than current surveys in the Euclid and CMB-S4 experiments.

The motivation for this research stems from the vulnerability of machine learning models to subtle, yet deliberate manipulations in their input data. The paper presents a novel approach, drawing from Bayesian learning theory, to guarantee the detection of such manipulations within certain limitations. The method involves establishing a Bayesian classifier that can be Gurobi or CPLEX, leveraging state-of-the-art solvers for optimization. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, outperforming comparable methods in accurately identifying manipulated inputs.

This research investigates the dissemination patterns of online rumors in China during the COVID-19 pandemic. We analyzed a dataset comprising 10,000 rumors collected from Weibo, the most popular social media platform in China. Our findings reveal distinct characteristics of rumor spread mechanisms, with the majority of active accounts being those that posted early in the pandemic. In contrast to our previous study, we observed that the majority of accounts active during the pandemic had low posting frequencies. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that influence is multi-dimensional, encompassing factors such as network structure, content, and temporal influence. We developed the KNN-IUM model to accurately measure and compare the varying impacts of online rumors.

In remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging is a rapidly growing field. It involves capturing and analyzing the spectral responses of each pixel in an image, allowing for detailed identification of materials and characteristics in various applications, including forestry and agriculture. However, the large number of spectral bands in these images can lead to the curse of dimensionality, making them difficult to work with. In this context, we investigate the impact of reducing spectral dimensions on hyperspectral pixel classification. Using the Fisher Linear Discriminant Analysis, we decrease the number of bands in a remote sensing image while preserving its discriminative power. Our experiments are conducted on the MNIST dataset, where we evaluate the classification performance using support vector machines and compare the results to those obtained using the full hyperspectral image. Our findings reveal that dimensionality reduction can lead to a significant improvement in classification accuracy, with the optimal number of reduced dimensions yielding an accuracy of 99.09%, compared to an accuracy of 98.09% with the full hyperspectral image.

We introduce NCompre, a novel framework designed to enhance the storage efficiency of natural language models without affecting their performance. The NCompre system leverages a two-tier compression approach, incorporating a symbolic layer to represent the weights of the underlying neural network through a combination of operations and variables. The primary variables within this layer are then compressed using existing techniques, resulting in a significant reduction in the model's size. The compression of variables in the nCompre framework yields a model that can be easily expanded, achieving a substantial improvement in storage efficiency compared to the original model. Thorough experiments on various BERT models and NCompre has demonstrated a model size reduction of up to 3.36 times, while maintaining consistent results with the baseline models on multiple evaluation datasets.

A novel method called Protein-SHMS validates and refines protein structures by comparing experimental hydrogen chemical shift data with the ones predicted from the protein's three-dimensional structure. By accurately calculating chemical shifts through quantum mechanics, the method identifies discrepancies between the structure and the experiment, revealing structural inaccuracies and deviations from the expected values. These discrepancies can guide protein structure refinement and have shown promising results in refining the structure of cytochrome c and cytochrome c peroxidase, with the latter's refined structure showing an improved root-mean-square deviation compared to the experimentally determined one from X-ray crystallography.

In deep learning, the choice of loss function plays a crucial role in the training process, influencing the optimization of model parameters. Despite being a fundamental aspect, research into how different loss functions affect the final model performance is relatively limited. This study delves into the impact of loss functions on the classification performance of models, examining various factors such as dataset, feature extraction methods, and model architectures. By conducting a comprehensive analysis, this research provides valuable insights for practitioners when selecting the most suitable loss function for their deep learning models.

The functions themselves are derived from the conditions of the non-interacting ground state and the conditions of the ground state in the interacting scenario. The conditions of the parquet theory are then shown to be equivalent to the conditions for the non-interacting ground state. A method that uses quantum Monte Carlo to investigate the behavior of bosons interacting with an environment is developed and used to study the properties of a specific type of excitation in a material exhibiting charge density wave. This approach is applied to studying the excitation in a material called $\bf TiSe_2$ through the molecular dynamics method. The results show that the excitation in this material has properties that are consistent with experimental measurements, but it exhibits a collapse of the excitation gap below the critical temperature due to the effects of the environment. The excitation's behavior changes from a superfluid to a metal as the temperature decreases, which is consistent with the observed material properties. The method's ability to study materials without adjustable parameters is a significant advantage, as it can be used to investigate the properties of excitons in similar materials under varying conditions.

In the US, large cities rely on community safety reporting systems to process safety concerns such as crime and traffic incidents. Users who have these systems in place can submit their concerns, which are then reviewed and dispatched to the appropriate city department. Our research focuses on analyzing the text-based interactions between users and dispatchers within these systems, which are characterized by a high degree of complexity and a high volume of data. Specifically, we investigate the factors that influence dispatcher behavior and the level of detail provided by dispatchers, which in turn affects how effectively cities can respond to safety concerns. Through an examination of a substantial dataset comprising over 100,000 dispatcher submissions across four cities, we uncover critical insights into dispatcher behavior and its relationship with various factors, such as the mode of contact and time of submission. Our analysis also highlights the potential biases present in dispatcher submissions and emphasizes the importance of considering these biases when making policy decisions. Ultimately, our findings have significant implications for how cities can use these reporting systems to make data-driven decisions and improve safety outcomes for their communities.

We've developed a theoretical framework to examine the properties of nematic superconductors, specifically those that are both nematic and paramagnetic, in the context of a triplet state. Our analysis reveals that the magnetic susceptibility of these materials is not uniform and exhibits anisotropic properties, with distinct behaviors along the direction of the nodal planes and the axis perpendicular to them. Anisotropy within the nodal planes arises from the alignment of these planes themselves, whereas anisotropy perpendicular to the planes is influenced by the alignment of local spins along the normal direction. Additionally, we discovered that the anisotropic magnetic susceptibility can be characterized by Ginzburg-Landau coefficients, exhibiting anisotropic GL critical fields as well as anisotropic behavior in specific directions.

This paper proposes a minimax active learning algorithm designed to reduce the number of labeled data points needed while maintaining a low risk of model error. The method alternates between a learner that aims to minimize misclassification and an active selection process that targets samples providing the most information for model training. Specifically, the learner utilizes predictions from two predictive models, while the selection process identifies classes with low confidence scores from these models. Our analysis demonstrates that this algorithm's risk of error is bounded and converges at a rate comparable to fully supervised methods, with only a slight increase due to the use of active learning. Furthermore, empirical results show that our approach outperforms existing methods, achieving significant reductions in sample size for comparable model accuracy.

The level of complexity in music is influenced by the stylistic choices of composers in two key areas: pitch organization and rhythmic structure. This study aims to quantify the changes in these aspects of music composition from 1976 to 2016 by analyzing 1,000 compositions from the Grand Piano Competition in Moscow. By measuring the informational complexity of each piece, researchers found that while there was no overall trend in contemporary music, there were noticeable shifts in both rhythmic and compositional complexity. Interestingly, compositions with increasingly complex rhythms tended to show a decrease in other measures of complexity.

A novel class of stochastic processes, which modify a standard Poisson process, is introduced and studied. A specific subclass of these processes, characterized by a multi-entry mechanism, is derived from conditional time-translation invariance. Mathematical analysis of this subclass reveals that it can be represented in two distinct forms, both of which exhibit a particular property in relation to invariance. In contrast, one form of this process does not satisfy invariance and therefore cannot be effectively applied. A significant finding relates to the asymptotic behavior of this process, which is shown to converge towards a Gamma distribution under certain conditions.

This paper reinterprets the concept of harmony from a constructive perspective, using the framework of Computational Ludics to analyze the interaction between formulas, and demonstrates that a revised definition of harmony ensures consistent behavior in the Construction Game. The construction of a symmetric connection formula between interacting formulas can be achieved by analyzing the parallel development of their contexts, which must progress in a mutually compatible manner.

A prominent method for learning reward functions in complex environments involves asking a human operator to group similar data points. The challenge lies in the time it takes for humans to perform this task, as they have to evaluate each data point one by one. To speed up the process, we propose using time-series data visualizations to help humans identify clusters more quickly. By presenting multiple data samples simultaneously and highlighting representative data samples, we can reduce the time it takes for humans to complete this task. Our approach also leverages the way humans perceive groupings to improve the accuracy of the learned reward function. The proposed method has shown significant reductions in the time it takes for humans to complete this task, up to 80%, while maintaining the same level of accuracy.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

In a ideal two-dimensional fluid confined within a disc-shaped domain, we investigate the existence of specific swirly flow patterns, characterized by singularities at their center. This investigation focuses on solutions within the class of flows with specific topological features, represented by elements of the group Z. 

We demonstrate the existence of specific vortex configurations with central vortices of a specific charge when the topological index is non-zero. These configurations remain stable under small disturbances when the topological index is one. 

A central challenge in this investigation involves controlling the behavior of centrifugal forces acting on outwards trajectory as they move away from the singularity at the center. 

Our analysis also reveals that when the topological index exceeds one, certain forces acting on the trajectory will eventually become centripetal, causing it to curve inwards.

The goal of outcome modeling studies is to draw valid causal conclusions from observational data by accounting for confounding biases.  In situations where these biases are complex and highly dimensional, causal inference methods based on propensity scores can provide a more accurate representation by projecting the bias onto a lower dimensional space.  The standard approach uses propensity scores to create comparable groups, but this can be unreliable when the groups are imbalanced.  By incorporating machine learning algorithms, we can improve the balance and create more comparable groups.  The combination of machine learning and propensity score-based methods offers several advantages, including enhanced model performance and flexibility.  However, these methods can be challenging to implement due to the need for careful model selection and the potential for overfitting.  A recent approach uses the residual variance to adjust propensity score-based estimators, but this method has limitations in terms of convergence and may not always provide accurate estimates.  In contrast, we propose a new estimator that combines machine learning and propensity score-based methods to achieve more accurate and stable estimates.  The proposed estimator uses a two-step process to create comparable groups and then applies the difference-in-means estimator to estimate the treatment effect.  The first step involves using machine learning to predict the outcome and the residual variance, and the second step uses these predictions to create comparable groups.  The proposed estimator has several advantages, including improved convergence and more accurate estimates in terms of bias and variance.  The proposed estimator also provides a framework for understanding the relationship between machine learning

The $\tau$ lepton serves as an excellent testing ground for the Standard Model, with its unique characteristics allowing for highly precise measurements of theoretical predictions.  However, making accurate predictions for certain $\tau$ decays, particularly those involving photons, poses a significant challenge due to complex two-body final states.  This problem is further complicated by the need for highly precise lattice QCD calculations, with current predictions for some processes falling short of the anticipated sub-percent accuracy threshold.  In this context, recent theoretical and experimental developments are discussed in detail.

A laboratory-scale rotating annulus experiment was used to simulate the growth of geostrophic调整和 baroclinic instability, which are responsible for the formation of mid-latitude weather systems. By replicating two different initial conditions within the rotating annulus setup, we were able to observe the development of wave patterns in both experiments. A numerical model based on the Navier-Stokes equations was used to simulate the corresponding dynamics, which were then compared with the results from the physical experiment. This comparison allowed us to validate the numerical model and assess its accuracy in predicting the growth of wave patterns. The numerical model successfully captured the characteristics of baroclinic instability, including the development of wave patterns and the associated heat transfer processes. The agreement between the experimental and numerical results suggests that the numerical model is a reliable tool for studying the dynamics of baroclinic waves and other geophysical fluid phenomena.

A novel reparameterisation of extreme value models enables the direct Bayesian inference of rare event characteristics using Pechersky, Pechersky and Stephenson's (2018) method. We enhance inference by transforming extreme value model parameters into parameters that control threshold exceedance frequencies, which subsequently influence sample parameter values. This approach leverages the standard threshold exceedance assumption, resulting in a Generalised Pareto distribution and significantly simplifying the application. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to two datasets, thereby showcasing its ease of implementation and computational efficiency.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, significant research has been conducted to develop algorithms that are robust to corrupted data. A significant challenge arises when certain transitions in the dataset are invalid, such as out-of-distribution samples resulting from labeling errors. This study takes a step further by introducing the concept of adversarial corruption, which not only produces invalid but also invalidating transitions. The paper defines a specific measure of resistance to this type of corruption and demonstrates the theoretical limitations of achieving this resistance while maintaining good performance. The research also establishes conditions under which certain algorithms can achieve optimal resistance with minimal performance loss, such as the Fitted Q-evaluation algorithm. The study also investigates the robustness of several state-of-the-art algorithms on synthetic and real-world datasets, including the MuJoCo walking dataset, and finds that these algorithms are highly susceptible to adversarial corruption, even when the dataset is of high quality.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. A key aspect of this research is the development of a strategy to achieve controllability through impulse control, which involves solving a one-dimensional heat equation influenced by Dirac measures both internally and on a boundary that changes over time.

A key challenge in deploying NLP systems in the real world is identifying out-of-distribution data, which is characterized by anomalies that deviate from expected patterns. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the various forms of OOD data, including corruption, contamination, domain shifts, and synthetically generated examples. Additionally, it explores different methods for detecting OOD data, including density estimation, likelihood-based approaches, and neural network-based techniques. The authors present a detailed evaluation of the most effective algorithms across a range of contexts, including anomaly detection, data contamination, domain adaptation, and style transfer, and highlight the limitations of current research in this area.

In recent years, nanomotors powered by quantum tunneling have garnered significant attention due to their potential applications in controlled material manipulation. To address the lack of a comprehensive theoretical framework, we develop a model describing the movement of tunneling-driven Brownian motors, which consist of a molecular rotor attached to a stationary molecular driver, both embedded in a semiconductor matrix. The model incorporates key tunneling characteristics, such as stochastic energy release and position-dependent transport probabilities, as driving forces for directional motion. Furthermore, we analyze the influence of Brownian noise and asymmetry in the system's energy landscape on the tunneling process, taking into account the complex interplay between noise and the electron transfer process.

Building on a 2019 finding by Germain and Strichman about bidirectional dictionary transducers re-synchronizing in two directions, we explore and establish the conditions for the existence of bidirectional re-synchronization in one-way transducers, which is possible in one specific case but generally impossible. Furthermore, we identify a necessary and sufficient condition for a specific type of one-way transducers to be re-synchronized in a different direction, which has significant implications for the development of efficient dictionary transducers that are re-synchronized in both directions and support multiple bidirectional operations. Our main contribution is a new algorithm for converting two-way transducers that are re-synchronized in one direction but not the other, into specific types of one-way transducers that are re-synchronized in the other direction, which are possible for specific types of one-way transducers but generally impossible.

In the realm of combinatorics, the concept of polynomial multiplication is central, with the Br\"{u}nning-G\"{u}nt{c}howski approach providing a framework for understanding its application in solving real-world problems. Building upon Br\"{u}nning-G\"{u}ntchowski's work, we have developed an algorithm that accelerates the process of calculating a polynomial given its coefficients and a specific evaluation point, with a time complexity of O(d^(1+eps)) for any desired improvement, where eps can be as small as 0.043. This advancement is particularly relevant in the field of combinatorics, where the Br\"{u}nning-G\"{u}ntchowski model is used to represent a polynomial based on the coefficients of another polynomial. Although there have been previous attempts to speed up this process, our new algorithm represents a significant improvement, with a more efficient time complexity.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 marked a significant milestone in the study of cool extrasolar objects, as it allowed researchers to observe these celestial bodies for the first time. Since its initial detection, GJ 229B has been extensively studied using various telescopes, yielding precise measurements of its atmospheric properties. Despite these efforts, the exact composition of its atmosphere remains uncertain, prompting scientists to conduct a detailed spectral analysis of its visible and near-infrared spectrum. By combining data from multiple observations, researchers were able to refine the estimated distance to GJ 229B and determine its effective temperature, which is approximately 650 Kelvin. Furthermore, the study revealed that the atmospheric composition of GJ 229B is consistent with a metal-rich environment, as it contains higher amounts of certain molecules such as water vapor and carbon dioxide. Overall, the study provides valuable insights into the atmospheric dynamics of GJ 229B, which can be used to inform the study of similar extrasolar objects.

To search for the potential existence of the unique $0^{--}$ state, we employed lattice QCD with dynamical fermions. Our results indicate that the minimum energy configuration can be achieved through either a point-like arrangement of quarks or by quarks organized in a meson-baryon structure. The computational setup involved using the lattice SU(3) gauge theory with light quark masses, roughly equivalent to those of up and down quarks, on lattices with varying sizes. The derived bound state energies suggest that the mass of the $0^{--}$ channel lies above that of the $0^{--}$ single-hadron thresholds. The observed lightest states in our simulation exhibit characteristics consistent with an molecular-like meson-baryon composition.

A crucial goal for the LHCb experiment is to measure the phase and magnitude of the phase-space factor in the $\Delta B = 2$ transition between $c_3 \bar{d}$ and $\bar{c}_3 d$ charmed states. This factor can provide insight into new physics beyond the Standard Model. To achieve this, we need to precisely determine the mixing phase and decay width difference between the $c_3 \bar{d}$ and $\bar{c}_3 d$ states. This paper outlines the experimental methods used to measure these quantities and presents the current results obtained from data collected until Summer 2015.

Airborne disease transmission in confined areas is influenced by the dynamics of well-mixed air and the balance between filtration and re-emission of virus particles. Although the unsteady state of airflow in such environments is often complex, simplified models that assume uniform mixing are sometimes used to estimate transmission risks. The effectiveness of these models in predicting actual virus concentrations in the breath of an infected person and subsequent transmission rates has not been thoroughly evaluated. This study aims to address this gap by comparing the well-stirred model with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of an urban bus environment. By comparing the model's predictions of COVID-19 transmission with actual transmission rates, this study aims to determine the well-stirred model's utility in predicting disease transmission in confined spaces.

Researchers have used a shell-model approach to investigate the characteristics of certain Te isotopes, specifically their beta decay properties. By incorporating the shell-model code, they calculated the logft values and final state properties for beta decays involving even-odd parent nuclei. These calculations were then compared with experimental data, and the results showed good agreement. Notably, the researchers found that some previously unobserved transitions in $^{135}$Te beta decay were consistent with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, they determined the logft values for a set of previously unobserved forbidden transitions in $^{137}$Te beta decay.

Double-sided auctions are a common method used in financial markets to facilitate matching between buyers and sellers. However, the complex algorithms behind these processes often contain errors. Our research provides a sound foundation for verifying auction algorithms by introducing a formal model that can be applied to any verified double-sided exchange. Additionally, our work presents specific, enforceable rules for digital asset transfers, which ensure compliance with the intended matching outcomes. These rules are then applied in the form of smart contracts on blockchains to prevent unauthorized transactions. Our findings are demonstrated through successfully verified auction implementations on the Tezos blockchain, including open-order book and hidden-order auctions.

Using heavy quark effective theory, we analyze the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying the Adiabatic Approximation and a Schrödinger equation, to investigate their properties, including mass, radii, and coupling constants. Our results, presented in tables and graphs, are compared with existing studies and experimental data from the LHCb, demonstrating agreement with the HQET framework and other theoretical and experimental sources.

M. R. Drmota, D. Kurepa, and A. Sch\"{o}nhage proposed an interesting problem in their work. They defined a periodic decomposition of the positive integers based on the remainder of each integer when divided by some value, with each set of integers sharing the same remainder split into several subsets. The condition for this decomposition is that no element can be the sum of two different elements within the same set. The maximum number of sets in such a decomposition varies depending on the value used to divide the integers. The problem lies in finding the highest possible number of sets in this decomposition, denoted as f(k), for each value of k. The current research shows that f(k) is greater than or equal to the logarithm base 3 of k for all k greater than 1.

A data-driven technique called dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) is used to identify and separate the linear components in complex systems. However, in situations where data is high-dimensional, nonlinear relationships are present, or system dynamics change over time, DMD's performance is compromised. To improve its usability, researchers have developed kernel-based DMD (kDMD), which incorporates kernel methods to accurately reconstruct linear subsystems under challenging conditions. However, kDMD is limited to linear systems due to the requirement of satisfying the Meyer-Wielandt inequality. To overcome this limitation, a new optimization framework has been proposed that utilizes kernel methods to identify the most suitable kernel for reconstructing linear subsystems without violating this inequality. This new framework, called Linear and Nonlinear Disambiguation Optimization (LANDO), offers a data-driven solution to identify the optimal kernel-based reconstruction of linear subsystems in complex systems, even when nonlinearities and time-varying conditions are present.

The chess opening repertoire is explored in this study, focusing on its structure and dynamics as revealed by online community data from Lichess.org. By examining the distribution of openings across different levels of play and their similarities, insights are gained into the strategic decisions made by players when choosing their moves. A game-theoretic perspective is adopted to analyze the complexity and similarity of the decisions made in the openings, with results indicating that human decision-making exhibits quantifiable patterns of stability and convergence.

We've developed a novel approach to determine the masses of co-orbiting millisecond pulsars (Psrs) and their white dwarf companions by analyzing orbital decay rates. A database of 33 Psr-WD binaries with well-determined fundamental parameters was used to develop this approach, which relies on the AIC index to estimate the orbital decay rate and subsequently the mass of the Psrs. The resulting mass estimates for the Psrs ranged from 1.03 to 1.48 solar masses, with an average of 1.30 solar masses and a precision of approximately 0.07 solar masses.
